newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AIRLINE RATES. CHINA..
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AIRLINE RATES. CHINA..

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Airline insurance rates are not doing well. Delegates at an airline insurance conference in London had it spelled out to them that they are trading prices which are too low to sustain a long-term healthy business. Having clawed its way back from unrealistically low levels in the early 1990s, excess capacity is again fuelling rate reductions.
Prices must rise, they were told, for while future consolidation is likely, capacity reduction is not.

Despite advances in technology, air experts seem resigned to around 20 major jet losses a year for the foreseeable future. What has changed however, is that the average value of a unit of risk has gone from USD18 million in 1990 to USD36 million now.
A large number of North Americans have been killed in air accidents in the last three years, and this has been the largest single chunk of liability figures.
The whole process has become marginal. Underwriting is leading to losses, and insurers will often have to rely on investment income to keep them in the black.
That means few are building up catastrophe funds, and it is only the strength of insurers' balance sheets, not the premium base that is supporting the large policy limits demanded by airlines.
--oo0oo--
Surveys commissioned by companies have a habit of appearing self-serving, but this week's conclusions from Chubb that foreign insurers will make little impact in China seems a little hard to accept.
The comparison is that foreign insurers have been in Japan for the last 30 years and have only three percent of the market share.

But companies in 1997 are not as they were in 1967. Growth expectations are high, and new markets are seen as much more important than they used to be. In addition companies have much more global reach and are much more aggressive and competitive.

The very fact that U.S. insurers were able to create an international dispute with Japan over insurance market opportunities, so serious it required President Clinton to intervene, is a measure of how seriously such markets are taken.
The pace of change and the need to introduce a culture of insurance in China will be obstacles to foreign insurers, but it will not stop them doing everything they can.
--OO0OO--
